claims.text: Replacing traditional EAM references with an actively trained MLIP will improve reference–target phase-space overlap in high-temperature multicomponent HEAs.
Replacing EAM references with the proposed MLIP will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD.
HfNbTaTiZr is an equiatomic quinary refractory high-entropy alloy.
The proposed methodology applies to both solid and liquid HfNbTaTiZr near its melting point.
Approximately 1200 °C and above is an appropriate near-melting temperature range for the example HfNbTaTiZr system.
Active learning on diverse ab initio liquid snapshots can capture the full diversity of liquid atomic configurations.
The applicable compositional range is typically 4–7 elements in near-equiatomic ratios.
The applicable temperature range is at least 1200 °C.
High-temperature multicomponent HEA liquids exhibit a very broad distribution of atomic configurations.
Chemical short-range order is a material-relevant feature of HfNbTaTiZr.
An MLIP trained on ab initio liquid configurations will embed liquid short-range-order and disorder effects.
Embedding these effects will bridge the gap between EAM and ab initio phase spaces.
Training on a wide and representative set of ab initio liquid configurations will model the potential-energy surface more accurately.
A more accurate potential-energy surface will increase configurational overlap between the reference and ab initio target states.
Increased configurational overlap will reduce systematic thermodynamic-integration path errors relative to EAM.
The MLIP will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 30–50% relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
The reduction in path mismatch will produce more accurate free-energy estimates.
TOR-TILD uses EAM reference potentials that inadequately represent ab initio liquid configurations and consequently increase integration-path mismatch.
The intervention is effective only for complex multicomponent HEAs with high melting points, while simpler or lower-melting alloys should benefit less.
The magnitude of improvement depends on training-data quality, training-data diversity, and alloy identity.
